title: Understanding Dynamics of Adam in Zero-Sum Games: An ODE Approach
claim: A continuous-time approximation tracks the discrete adaptive algorithm closely, while a simplified sign-based limit diverges or reaches different equilibria on some problems.
layout: 3 panels side-by-side, shared legend style, trajectories over gray vector-field streamlines
description: Three side-by-side 2-D phase-plane plots, each showing a different test game. Light gray streamlines with arrows show the underlying vector field. Over them are three trajectories: a thick dashed gray-blue line for discrete Adam-DA, a thin dark navy line for Continuous Adam-DA, and a magenta line for SignGDA Flow. A star marks the shared start point. In the left panel, all curves loop around a polygon-shaped limit cycle and roughly agree. In the middle panel, the navy and dashed curves spiral inward to the center equilibrium, while the magenta curve traces an enlarging diamond and does not converge. In the right panel, the navy and dashed curves converge to the upper equilibrium, while the magenta curve goes to the lower one. A legend sits inside each panel, and the axes are labeled x and y.

Especially in [ref] and [ref], where [ref] either diverges or approaches to a different equilibrium, while the trajectories of the other two methods remain similar. More details are provided in Appendix [ref].
abstract: The remarkable success of the Adam in training neural networks has naturally led to the widespread use of its descent-ascent counterpart, Adam-DA, for solving zero-sum games. Despite its popularity in practice, a rigorous theoretical understanding of Adam-DA still lags behind. In this paper, we derive ordinary differential equations (ODEs) that serve as continuous-time limits of the Adam-DA. These ODEs closely approximate the discrete-time dynamics of Adam-DA, providing a tractable analytical framework for understanding its behavior in zero-sum games. Using this ODE approach, we investigate two fundamental aspects of Adam-DA: local convergence and implicit gradient regularization. Our analysis reveals that the roles of the first- and second-order momentum parameters in zero-sum games are exactly the opposite of their well-documented effects in minimization problems. We validate these predictions through GAN experiments across multiple architectures and datasets, demonstrating the practical implications of this reversed momentum effect.
